content: The provided text is a detailed dataset and analysis of studies related to people who inject drugs (PWID), general populations, high-risk groups, prisoners, and people living with HIV (PLHIV). It includes information on study characteristics, outcomes, and models of care for hepatitis C virus (HCV) testing and treatment. 1. Study Populations and Locations: Studies were conducted across various global regions, including Europe, Africa, the Americas, South-East Asia, the Western Pacific, and the Eastern Mediterranean. Populations studied included PWID, homeless individuals, prisoners, PLHIV, and general or high-risk populations. Countries involved included Norway, the United Kingdom, Mozambique, Georgia, Myanmar, India, France, Thailand, South Africa, Nigeria, Pakistan, Egypt, Ukraine, and Cambodia. 2. Study Designs: The studies employed prospective and retrospective observational designs, with some using cluster non-randomized interventions. Data sources included WHO contact databases, conference abstract searches, and Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) partnerships. 3. HCV Testing and Treatment Models: The studies evaluated point-of-care (PoC) RNA assays and laboratory-based assays for HCV diagnosis and treatment initiation. PoC RNA assays were conducted either on-site or via mobile units, while lab-based assays were performed off-site. Models of care were categorized based on whether testing and treatment occurred at the same site or different sites, and whether they were completed during the same visit or on different days. 4. HCV Cascade of Care Outcomes: The cascade of care included HCV antibody testing, RNA testing, pre-treatment assessment, treatment initiation, and sustained virological response (SVR12) at 12 weeks post-treatment. Weighted HCV RNA prevalence among those tested for anti-HCV varied by population group: PWID and homeless individuals: 16% (12–21%). General populations and high-risk groups: 10% (5–17%). Prisoners: 6% (4–10%). PLHIV: 5% (3–8%). 5. Key Findings: PoC RNA assays demonstrated high feasibility and effectiveness, with many studies reporting 100% RNA testing completion rates. Treatment initiation rates varied but were generally higher in PoC models compared to lab-based models. SVR12 rates were consistently high across studies, often exceeding 80% in PoC arms. Mobile PoC units were particularly effective in reaching underserved populations, such as homeless individuals and PWID. 6. Global and Regional Insights: Studies from lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) accounted for 47% of the total, highlighting the global burden of HCV in resource-limited settings. European studies dominated the dataset, comprising 50% of the total studies. The Eastern Mediterranean region had the highest proportion of studies focused on high-risk populations. 7. Study Characteristics: A total of 45 studies with 64 study arms were included, with 36% of studies having two or more arms. PoC RNA assay arms were more prevalent (45 arms) compared to lab-based arms (19 arms). Models of care varied, with some studies achieving same-site, same-visit testing and treatment initiation, while others required multiple visits or different sites. 8. Implications for HCV Elimination: The findings underscore the importance of PoC testing and treatment models in improving HCV care cascades, particularly in marginalized populations. Mobile PoC units and same-visit models of care are critical for reducing barriers to HCV diagnosis and treatment. The high SVR12 rates achieved in these studies demonstrate the potential for scaling up PoC interventions to achieve global HCV elimination targets. This interpretation provides a comprehensive understanding of the dataset, emphasizing the significance of PoC testing and treatment models in addressing HCV among vulnerable populations globally.
